reason: This passage recounts Amnon's assault on his sister Tamar and the immediate aftermath. No character in the text is presented as modeling good leadership with humility in the face of criticism. King David hears of the crime and becomes very angry (v. 36), but the passage shows no demonstration of humble response, appropriate discipline of his son Amnon, or corrective leadership action. Amnon exhibits lust, deception, and cruelty; Absalom harbors silent hatred and harbors revenge; Jonadab acts with cunning manipulation. The narrative focuses on documenting a grave crime and the emotional responses it provokes, not on exemplifying virtuous leadership.
